content.p: The Hells Angels Motorcycle Club is an outlaw motorcycle club. Its name turns up in rock history, in a Quebec gang war that had claimed more than 150 lives by 2000, and in court cases in Canada and the United States.
content.h2: The Oakland chapter and Sonny Barger
content.p: Consequence, reporting on the death of Sonny Barger in June 2022, describes him as the founder of the original Oakland chapter, which he started in 1957. The same article says the San Bernardino chapter, formed in 1947, is often credited as the first, while the Oakland chapter was the most influential. Consequence gives both dates and says the Oakland chapter "may not have been the first." It does not explain the difference, so the question of who came first remains open.

Barger was born on 8 October 1938 as Ralph Hubert Barger Jr. According to Consequence, his gruff manner and his sayings made him one of the faces of the counterculture of the 1960s, and his business sense turned the club into a financial force. The article says the Hells Angels name appeared on products from T-shirts to wine. Barger died at 83. A statement posted on his official Facebook page, which he had asked be published after his death, said he had passed peacefully after a brief battle with cancer.

The club's name entered the history of popular music at a free concert at Altamont Speedway in California on 6 December 1969. Consequence says about 300,000 people came to the event, which was billed as "Woodstock West," with the Rolling Stones as headliners. The Grateful Dead had been scheduled to play before the Stones but pulled out as the crowd became more violent.

The Stones had moved the concert at short notice after other venues fell through. A feature by Classical Music says the band wanted to avoid a police presence, partly because of an ongoing series of drug busts, and that it therefore asked the Hells Angels to handle security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. The same article says the club had handled security at earlier free concerts in San Francisco, including the Human Be-In of January 1967, but that the Altamont site was poorly prepared, with no adequate toilets, no medical tents, and no food or water.

The feature describes the violence in the crowd. It says Hells Angels fought fans during the opening sets, that Jefferson Airplane's singer Marty Balin was knocked unconscious when he tried to calm things, and that Stephen Stills of Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young was stabbed in the leg during that group's set. These are the feature's own descriptions of events, and the other reports cited here do not confirm them in detail.

The most serious incident happened during the Stones' set. The feature says Meredith Hunter, an 18-year-old from Berkeley, approached the stage, was pushed back by members hired to keep fans away, and then returned with a revolver. It says he was stabbed and beaten by Alan Passaro, a Hells Angels member. Passaro was tried in 1971 and acquitted. The feature says the jury found self-defence after viewing footage that showed Hunter drawing his gun. Filmmakers Albert and David Maysles shot footage of the concert, which appeared in their 1970 Stones documentary Gimme Shelter, according to the same article.

Accounts of responsibility differ. The feature reports that Jagger said the band had not known of the killing, and it quotes Barger describing the day as "just another Hells Angels event." Rolling Stone magazine, the feature says, called the concert a mix of "diabolical egotism, hype, ineptitude, money manipulation" and a lack of concern for humanity. Each of these is a judgement by a person or outlet, and none of them settles the question of blame.

In Quebec, the club's name is tied to a much darker conflict. The Christian Science Monitor, writing in September 2000, traced the war to 1994, when the Hells Angels tried to take over the rival Rock Machine while the Rock Machine's leader was in jail awaiting extradition to the United States on drug charges. The Rock Machine turned the offer down, and car bombs and shootings followed. The Monitor reported that the conflict had claimed more than 150 lives since 1994, and it quoted an opposition politician asking who was winning the war, with no convictions yet recorded.

The Monitor described the scale of the club itself in Canada. It estimated about 250 full-fledged members across the country, and 2,000 to 3,000 associates. It said the Quebec chapters behaved differently from those in western Canada, where a criminologist told the paper that some members were criminally involved but did not commit crimes as a chapter. The same report says an Alberta judge had ruled that a "zero tolerance" police operation against the club violated members' Charter rights.

The violence reached the press too. The Monitor reported that Michel Auger, an investigative reporter with the Journal de Montreal, was shot five times in the back in the parking lot of his newspaper. It was recovering under police guard when the paper wrote.

Quebec's response built towards the 2001 sweep. The Globe and Mail reported on 29 March 2001 that about 2,000 officers in three provinces reported that the raids on clubhouses and homes had taken place at dawn the day before. In Montreal alone, 87 suspects were due to be arraigned by videolink. Most members of the Nomads chapter, the Globe reported, were arrested, according to their lawyer. Among those named in the papers were Walter Stadnick and Richard Mayrand, both former national presidents of the club in Canada.

The Globe reported that the police alleged that Maurice "Mom" Boucher, already in custody awaiting trial on charges of ordering the killing of two prison guards, had masterminded the killing of at least 15 people. Police added 13 murder counts and three attempted-murder counts against him. Francis Boucher, his son, faced a murder charge tied to eight of the same deaths. The Globe reported that most of the dead were rival bikers and that one man was shot by mistake. These were allegations, and the Globe's wording reflects that.

The Globe and Mail reported that Stadnick and Donald Stockford were among the last of those arrested in the 2001 sweep to face trial. Both were Hamilton men and, the paper said, members of the Nomads chapter in Montreal. Stockford had been arrested at his home in Ancaster, outside Hamilton, during the 2001 operation.

In September 2004 Quebec Superior Court Justice Jerry Zigman sentenced both men to 20 years in prison. The Globe reported that a jury had found them guilty in June on five counts, among them a conspiracy to commit murder, drug trafficking and gangsterism. Stadnick had earlier been cleared of 13 murder counts and three attempted-murder counts. The Crown had asked for 24-year terms, and the defence had proposed between 13 and 15 years.

The judge called the two men violent and said they had expressed no remorse. Crown prosecutor Randall Richmond told reporters the sentences were among the heaviest given to any people. The Globe reported that 32 other Hells Angels members and associates had been convicted, and that Richmond cited 109 convictions in all. Given the parole rules, the paper calculated that the two men would spend at least a decade behind bars before they could be released.

The Globe also reported financial evidence. Records taken from the club's drug accounts showed that in 2000 Stockford and Stadnick spent more than $11 million buying cocaine and hashish through a drug consortium called La Table. The Crown sought fines of $11 million, believed by the Globe to be the largest in Canadian history, along with forfeiture of cars, cash and part of each man's home.

The Justice Department's Western District of Washington described its December 2008 case against members of the club's Nomads chapter in Washington State as the first RICO jury verdicts against a notorious outlaw motorcycle club in twenty years.

The department said the case followed a ten-week trial. It reported that Rodney Rollness was sentenced to life in prison, that Joshua Binder received 15 years, and that Rick Fabel, president of the chapter, was sentenced to more than seven years. The department quoted U.S. Attorney Jeffrey C. Sullivan, who said the trial team had "pierced the culture of silence and intimidation" the group used to hide its activities. The statement was issued to recognise the trial team, so that description is the department's own account.

Outlaw clubs have fought each other as well as the police. In May 2015 a brawl at the Twin Peaks restaurant in Waco, Texas, left nine bikers dead. NBC News reported that the first criminal trial stemming from it ended in a mistrial in November 2017. The defendant, Christopher "Jake" Carrizal, president of the Bandidos' Dallas chapter, testified that the Cossacks had provoked the fight. Jurors deliberated for 14 hours before the judge declared a mistrial. NBC also reported that local police arrested 177 bikers after the fighting and that more than 150 people were eventually charged. NBC calls the brawl the deadliest shootout between biker groups in U.S. history and describes the Cossacks as a rival club. It is included here only as context for the rivalries between clubs, not as part of the Hells Angels record.

The club's history now sits between two accounts. One is the account of the courts and police, which in Quebec and Washington State produced convictions, long sentences and a demand for $11 million in fines. The other is the account of the club's own figures: Barger called Altamont "just another Hells Angels event," and his post-death statement described the club as "an amazing club."

The questions the saved reports leave open include the full toll of the Quebec war, which the Monitor gave only as more than 150 lives by 2000; the club's total membership, which the Monitor estimated only for Canada; and how far responsibility for the death at Altamont lay with the band, the club and the concert's poor planning.
